In an eight-week trial in two of its buildings, Elm Quay Housing entered repair reports into a shared log from Svale Systems. This account follows how the maintenance team set it up, what its internal figures do and do not show, and what its supervisor would do differently.

By Thomas

Telephone repair reports and emails used to be stored separately at Elm Quay Housing, which manages 640 flats. In September 2025 its maintenance team decided to trial a shared repair log in two buildings. An internal trial note and the maintenance supervisor's own assessment record how it went.

## Why Elm Quay chose a shared log

Before settling on Svale Systems as its supplier, the team tested whether the log could show the status of each repair.

Maya Lind, the maintenance supervisor, was interviewed by email. "We wanted the evening shift to see what the morning shift had already done," she says. "The categories were ours; Svale helped us put them into the log."

## Six staff learn the log before the trial

Residents could still report repairs by telephone. Svale configured the log and trained six staff during two sessions, and the trial ran for eight weeks.

"We spent more time agreeing on the categories than entering the first reports," Lind says of the preparation. "I would set that time aside before the next building starts."

## The trial note leaves the cause open

Elm Quay's internal trial note, dated December 4, 2025, counts 31 repair reports entered, excluding emergencies and work ordered before the trial began. Median time from report to assignment was two working days during the trial, against three in the preceding eight weeks.

The two periods had different workloads, and the note explicitly does not attribute the difference to the software. Costs, resident satisfaction and completion times were not measured.

## Lind looks back on the eight weeks

"I would choose to do the trial again. Having one view of the reports helps us, but I would leave an extra week for preparation," she says.

Lind stops short of recommending Svale to every housing company. The trial has not yet been extended beyond the two buildings; the team will decide after checking how its categories work for larger repairs.

## Read the checklist before a trial of your own

The eight weeks left Elm Quay with figures its own note does not credit to the software and an assessment with a condition attached. # Elm Quay's maintenance shifts share one repair log

In an eight-week trial in two of its buildings, Elm Quay Housing entered repair reports into a shared log from Svale Systems. This account follows how the maintenance team set it up, what its internal figures do and do not show, and what its supervisor would do differently.

By Thomas

Telephone repair reports and emails used to be stored separately at Elm Quay Housing, which manages 640 flats. In September 2025 its maintenance team decided to trial a shared repair log in two buildings. An internal trial note and the maintenance supervisor's own assessment record how it went.

## Why Elm Quay chose a shared log

Before settling on Svale Systems as its supplier, the team tested whether the log could show the status of each repair.

Maya Lind, the maintenance supervisor, was interviewed by email. "We wanted the evening shift to see what the morning shift had already done," she says. "The categories were ours; Svale helped us put them into the log."

## Six staff learn the log before the trial

Residents could still report repairs by telephone. Svale configured the log and trained six staff during two sessions, and the trial ran for eight weeks.

"We spent more time agreeing on the categories than entering the first reports," Lind says of the preparation. "I would set that time aside before the next building starts."

## The trial note leaves the cause open

Elm Quay's internal trial note, dated December 4, 2025, counts 31 repair reports entered, excluding emergencies and work ordered before the trial began. Median time from report to assignment was two working days during the trial, against three in the preceding eight weeks.

The two periods had different workloads, and the note explicitly does not attribute the difference to the software. Costs, resident satisfaction and completion times were not measured.

## Lind looks back on the eight weeks

"I would choose to do the trial again. Having one view of the reports helps us, but I would leave an extra week for preparation," she says.

Lind stops short of recommending Svale to every housing company. The trial has not yet been extended beyond the two buildings; the team will decide after checking how its categories work for larger repairs.

## Read the checklist before a trial of your own

The eight weeks left Elm Quay with figures its own note does not credit to the software and an assessment with a condition attached. Operations managers weighing a shared log can start with the [implementation checklist](https://example.invalid/svale/checklist), a document to read before planning a trial.
EOF

## Findings (source support)

**F1. Title: the subject has changed from the team to the shifts.**
- Draft: "Elm Quay's maintenance shifts trial a shared log"
- Source: "its own maintenance team decided to trial a shared repair log"; "The team wanted staff on different shifts to see the same information."
- In the source, the team ran the trial. The shifts appear only as its aim: the team wanted staff on different shifts to see the same information.
- Concrete case: the six trained staff all worked morning shifts, and evening-shift staff took no part in the trial. The material does not exclude this. Lind says the team "wanted" the evening shift to see the morning shift's work, not that both shifts used the log. In that case the source holds and the title fails.
- Repair: "Elm Quay's maintenance team trials a shared log".

**F2. Section heading: "trained" has become "learn".**
- Draft: "Six staff learn the log in two sessions"
- Source: "Svale configured the log and trained six staff during two sessions."
- The source reports that training was given, not what the staff learned.
- Concrete case: six staff attended two training sessions but had not yet mastered the log. This is compatible with the material, and nothing supplied excludes it. In that case the source holds and the heading fails.
- Repair: "Six staff trained in two sessions".

**F3. Section heading: "does not credit the software" is wider than the source.**
- Draft: "The trial note does not credit the software"
- Source: "the note explicitly does not attribute the difference to the software."
- The source limits the non-attribution to the difference in median time to assignment. The heading extends it to the software in general.
- Concrete case: the note credits the log with making repair status visible across shifts, while explicitly not attributing the change in assignment time to it. Nothing supplied excludes this, because the material does not give the note's full contents. In that case the source holds and the heading fails.
- Repair: "The trial note does not credit the software with the difference", or "The trial note does not attribute the shorter assignment time to the software".

**F4. Lind's reservation: "stops short of" adds a stance.**
- Draft: "She stops short of recommending Svale to every housing company."
- Source: "Lind did not recommend Svale to every housing company."
- "Stops short of" suggests that Lind went some way towards recommending Svale. The source records only that she did not recommend it to every housing company. Her quotations endorse repeating the trial and one view of the reports; they do not recommend Svale as such.
- Concrete case: Lind made no recommendation of Svale to anyone. This is compatible with the material: the only statements are that she did not recommend Svale to every company, and her quotations, none of which recommend Svale. In that case the source holds, but the draft misstates her stance.
- Repair: "She did not recommend Svale to every housing company."
